label: a6-120-cex-open-bounded-euclidean-subset-not-compact
tail:
### FINDING 1 — FATAL — location: [L2] / step 1.2
CLAIM AS WRITTEN: "[L2] The unit vector $e_0$ exists and has Euclidean norm $1$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]])."
WHY IT FAILS: The quoted statement of `lem-standard-basis-of-f-n` defines standard unit vectors in $F^n$ and proves they form an ordered basis; it **never defines a norm, does not mention “Euclidean norm”, and asserts nowhere that any vector has norm $1$.** The relevant portion reads:
> “For $i < n$ define the **standard unit vector** $e_i \in F^{n}$ by
> $$e_i(i) = 1_F, \qquad e_i(j) = 0_F \ \text{ for } j < n \text{ with } j \ne i .$$”
The lemma is purely algebraic. The citation therefore ascribes to it a claim it does not make. In step 1.2 the unlicensed “Euclidean norm 1” is used to conclude $e_0 \notin B_2(0,1)$ and to compute $d(e_0,(1-\varepsilon)e_0)=\varepsilon$; without it the proof that the ball is not closed is unsupported.
WHAT WOULD FIX IT: Either cite a definition of the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb{R}^n$ together with a lemma that the standard basis vectors have norm $1$, or compute the distance directly from the definition of the Euclidean metric (which must itself be cited).

### FINDING 2 — FATAL — location: steps 1.1, 1.2, [L3], and the overall proof
CLAIM AS WRITTEN: The proof uses the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its specific distance properties, e.g. in step 1.2:
> “for every $r>0$ the point $(1-\varepsilon)e_0$, with $0<\varepsilon<\min(r,1)$, lies in both $B_2(0,1)$ and $B_2(e_0,r)$.”
The notation $B_2$ is employed throughout, and step 1.1 appeals to “distance less than 1 … from 0”.
WHY IT FAILS: **None of the cited dependencies defines the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb{R}^n$ or the notation $B_2$.**  
`def-metric-ball` defines $B(x,r)$ for an arbitrary metric space $(X,d)$:
> “$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}$.”
It does not specify a metric for $\mathbb{R}^n$ and does not define the subscript $2$. The other dependencies (`def-metric-topology`, the Heine–Borel theorem, `lem-standard-basis-of-f-n`) likewise supply no metric on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Consequently the assertions “the open unit ball is bounded” (step 1.1) and “it is not closed” (step 1.2) are not logically derived from the declared Facts and Assumptions; they depend on unstated definitions and properties of the Euclidean distance.
WHAT WOULD FIX IT: Add a dependency that defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ as a metric space with the Euclidean distance (e.g., the $\ell^2$ norm) and either provides or permits the basic distance calculations used in the proof.

2 fatal, 0 nonfatal
